content:
I lack academic excellence.
On the first day I was hospitalized, I instinctively diagnosed two patients with ASD and ADHD. The one with ASD lives in room 1, while the one with ADHD occupies room 13. The girl with ASD showed me her room right after I moved in; her phone rang incessantly, to the point that she seemed to vibrate along with it. The sharp ringtones struck her like electric shocks, causing her fingers to flap like butterfly wings. She asked me to help her turn off the alarm.
The boy with ADHD, on the other hand, was constantly by my side, talking endlessly about nothing. He’s a nice person, especially since he speaks English the entire time, although most of what I hear is just noise from my own brain due to the hallucinations I experience. He told me that the only way to escape this place is to get married. When you feel the urge to marry someone, you go to the place that has the only connection to the outside world – it’s like a cage in a garden, with a lighter fixed on its right side. When you press the tiny button in the center, a bright red circle lights up, faint like a distress signal. Then you wait, quietly, with a lit cigarette. If the other person comes, you share the cigarette in the cage, and if you still want to get married after finishing it, you register your names. Otherwise, you throw the cigarette butt to the ground.
Smoke happens when something is on fire.
Smoking is terrible for your health. A small, fleeting cigarette held in your mouth, burned by the lighter, with its flickering light crawling slowly. Light is often seen as hope, but it’s unfortunate that tar and nicotine hidden in the smoke secretly infiltrate your body. You tell yourself what a peaceful world this is. Then, somehow, the cigarette is finished, and you return to living however you want, though the tar, accumulated over time, continues to damage you with each breath.
There are so many lighters in the world, big and small, much like people’s fleeting crushes for various reasons. Some ignite their hope in a moment of impulse, while others are simply addicted. The common thread is that “life can be boring anywhere.”
And so they share the same ending – a scene littered with cigarette butts and bodies strewn across the ground.
Smoking is the worst thing you could ever start.
I saw many people heading to the cage to smoke while I stood by the gate, watching them pace back and forth like trapped monsters. There’s clearly a chair there, yet no one sits.
Is it because there’s only one chair?
I don’t know how to smoke.
People who don’t smoke should still have the right to marry. So, the other option is to place your drink on top of the trash bin next to the chair. If your partner wants to marry you, they can drink it.
I saw a few cups sitting on that trash bin. Sometimes they held hand cream; sometimes coffee; and sometimes just a lone bottle of vitamin drink with a name on it. How strange – why put a name on it if you don’t plan to drink it?
I sit in the chair, holding a glass of water inside this cage, facing many windows. This setup reveals all the struggles that people who drink and smoke endure, yet they can never escape.
But no, he said the only way to escape is to get married.
He’s wrong, of course. He probably thinks that way because he has ADHD.
The hospital room numbers contain a secret code. For those with ASD, the smaller number comes first, while for ADHD, it’s the opposite. This means that only the two rooms at the end of the hallway have the power to invite others to live with them. He lives in room 13, which is not at the end of the hallway, even though it’s close to the cage. I live in room 3, which is near the exit.
I lack academic excellence because later, I realized that both of my patients were simply bipolar.
Bipolar disorder is like a candle that burns at both ends. It’s nothing more than just a thinner story.
